title: Primitive words and context-freeness
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
why: The primitive-word language is a basic boundary case linking periodicity of words with the expressive power of context-free grammars.
status_note: Explicitly open in the STACS 2026 introduction and retained on the checked author problem list. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the probabilistic-membership result is a different target and no general context-freeness resolution was identified.

progress.text: The STACS paper treats context-freeness of primitive words as a longstanding open question; its probabilistic-membership theorem does not resolve it.

importance.reason: A canonical elementary language whose grammar expressibility remains a fundamental question in combinatorics on words and automata theory.

sentences: A primitive word is nonempty and is not a power of any shorter nonempty word.
The language contains all such words over a fixed finite alphabet with at least two symbols.
The conjecture says that no context-free grammar generates exactly this language.
Grammars may be ambiguous, so unique-parse limitations would not settle the question.
A 2026 paper still states this grammar-expressibility question as open.

definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Primitivity excludes every nontrivial repetition of a shorter word. The question asks whether a context-free grammar can express that condition over all lengths.
The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains context-freeness of primitive words as open while proving a result about probabilistic membership.

notes: Recovered the universal finite-alphabet quantifier and excluded the empty word explicitly. Defined proper powers and unrestricted finite context-free grammars.
Kept ordinary context-freeness separate from unambiguous or deterministic context-freeness and from membership algorithms.
Checked the February 2026 primary paper’s explicit open-status remark; supplied dated progress, significance and Lean criterion.
